nameStory: The Eastern Ashen Reticulated Beetle gets its name from the distinctive net-like pattern covering its wing covers, which reminded early entomologists of a fishing net or lattice work. The 'ashen' part refers to its grayish coloration, like the color of wood ash, while 'reticulated' comes from the Latin word for net.
description: The Eastern Ashen Reticulated Beetle is a small, ancient-looking beetle with a distinctive net-like pattern etched across its back. These beetles are part of one of the most primitive beetle families still alive today, essentially living fossils that have changed little over millions of years. They're typically small to medium-sized beetles with a somewhat flattened appearance and muted grayish-brown coloring. You'll need to look closely to appreciate their intricate surface patterns, as they're not particularly flashy insects.

idTips.label: Net-like wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for a distinctive raised grid or honeycomb pattern covering the wing covers (elytra) that feels bumpy to the touch, like running your finger over fine mesh

idTips.label: Grayish-brown coloring
idTips.description: Overall ashen gray to brownish color, similar to weathered wood or dried leaves, helping them blend into bark crevices

idTips.label: Primitive antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like or slightly saw-toothed antennae that are proportionally long for their body size, unlike the clubbed antennae of many other beetles

idTips.label: Flattened body shape
idTips.description: Somewhat compressed appearance that allows them to slip into tight spaces under bark, feeling firm but not as rounded as many beetles

idTips.label: Slow, deliberate movement
idTips.description: Moves methodically rather than scurrying quickly when disturbed, often freezing in place when first uncovered

habitat: Eastern Ashen Reticulated Beetles live under the bark of dead or dying hardwood trees, particularly favoring oak, maple, and birch in New England's mixed forests. They prefer moist, shaded woodland areas where fallen logs and standing dead trees (snags) provide plenty of hiding spots. You'll most often find them by carefully peeling back loose bark from recently fallen trees or examining wood piles that have been sitting for a season or two.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under bark. This is an excellent time to find them by examining loose bark on dead trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be found moving about under bark or occasionally on wood surfaces during humid evenings.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare for winter by burrowing deeper into bark crevices and decaying wood. Still findable but becoming less active as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, overwintering as adults deep in bark crevices or rotting wood. Rarely seen unless you disturb their winter shelters on warmer days.

funFact: These beetles are living time capsules - their family has remained virtually unchanged for over 200 million years, making them older than dinosaurs and among the most primitive beetles still crawling around today!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with click beetles or small longhorn beetles found in similar dead wood habitats. The key difference is the distinctive raised net pattern on reticulated beetles - run your finger across their back and you'll feel the bumpy grid, while other beetles have smooth or differently textured wing covers.
contextualKnowledge: The family name Cupedidae comes from an old genus name, and these beetles represent one of the four main evolutionary lineages of beetles. Finding one is like discovering a living piece of ancient natural history right in your local woods.
compareHints: As the only Tenomerga species in New England, this beetle is most easily compared to other reticulated beetles in different genera, though none are common in our region. The Eastern Ashen stands out from other primitive beetle families by its characteristic reticulated pattern and preference for hardwood rather than coniferous trees. Unlike more modern beetle families, it lacks the specialized features like clubbed antennae or bright warning colors.
